name: t99_bb_stretch
headline: AI Detected
windows:
Some families run on a bargain like “If I’m happy while someone I love is suffering, I’m abandoning them.”
That’s exactly why I was crying for 14 years. Beginning at the age of 12, when I really started to understand that life is brutal for most people, I became convinced that being happy myself, while others weren’t, was selfish. I had this poster in my room that really resonated with me, by the famous socialist, Eugene V.

I told this to a therapist in college and she actually agreed it was a good reason to be depressed!
What I found, once I started cultivating my own happiness, was that I got a lot better at helping other people toward theirs.
That might not be how it goes for everyone, and it doesn’t mean unhappy people can’t help.
I’d still take real suffering seriously, and do what you owe the people around you, but skip the part where you have to be miserable too.
Some friends or family really might not like it when you get happier, though.
Someone might pull away, or keep dragging you back into the old misery. I’d take that loss seriously, and look at what they do and what you owe them, before deciding it’s envy.
I’d still try a small good thing, like a nice meal, and see what actually happens.

Blowing up their phone and sulking all night is a different story.
Your Guide could help you ask for what you need instead, like a hug before they go and a rough idea of when they’ll be back.

name: t99_guide_stretch
headline: AI Detected
windows: I think the opposite trap can feel a lot like finally having your act together.
It’s forced adulthood, and it sounds like “Nope, all good!” from somebody with a fever who’s cleaning the whole kitchen anyway.
Not a lot of fun in that kitchen, and nobody gets very close to the person in it.
If that’s you, clamping down harder is going to feel like the fix, but it’s just more of the same.

I’d try croaking to someone you trust, “Could you pick up some soup?” If you keep swinging between spoiling and clamping down, try staying warm while you say what happens next, like “Not now, we’ll go after lunch.”
Once a need does show, after all that hiding, it’s okay to want a lot of closeness. So then someone you love goes for a walk alone, and you’ve texted “hello??” before they’re at the corner.
When they get back, you sulk all night. Wanting them close is fine! Blowing up their phone and sulking all night is a different story.
Your Guide could help you ask for what you need instead, like a hug before they go and a rough idea of when they’ll be back.
Before any of that, though, I’d let your little one say what’s going on.
I think it just wants to know they’re coming back.
The Guide doesn’t need to know everything for sure (that would be an OCD Guide, and then you’d need a Guide for the OCD Guide).
It chooses the next sane step that fits your values based on the info available, and that’s how it helps your little one grow toward a whole life.
Waiting to be sure first is sometimes proper & prudent, but if it’s a pattern, it can keep life on hold, and then your little one’s world stays small.

Sometimes something really is stuck on someone else’s end (you’ve asked, and followed up, and there’s nothing left for you to do yet), and waiting on that isn’t avoidance. The Guide can let it wait, keeping an eye out for when it frees up, and keep the rest of your life moving, so your little one keeps growing anyway.

name: t99_ended_stretch
headline: Human Written
windows:
When One Life Has Ended and the Next Hasn’t Begun
Your little one can get really loud in the gap after one life ends and before the next one has formed. A breakup will do it, or moving to another country, an illness, losing your faith or a role, your youngest moving out. So can leaving a family or a community, or staying but on new terms.
Even a therapist or helper stepping back, once you’ve grown a lot, can set it off.
In Tibetan Buddhism there’s a word for an in-between state like this: a bardo.

I’m not asking you to believe what they teach about death and rebirth. The word is just handy for that weird stretch after an ending, when the old you is gone and the new you hasn’t shown up yet.
Your little one might be sure everything’s over. Is it?

Usually one real thing ended, and there’s other stuff you’re still trying to keep going, maybe on autopilot. Some of it just isn’t known yet, and unknown isn’t the same as gone. Ask your little one what they’re scared will happen in the meantime (worst-case scenarios are kind of their specialty).
Something basic can mark the ending, like boxing up the old keys. Nobody needs to know what door will open next. But when the not-knowing feels too heavy, a new identity can sure look tempting. Like a borrowed coat that doesn’t fit but at least it’s warm.
But you can’t go far with a borrowed coat anyway, so don’t force the future on. Keep taking care of yourself, and grieve what ended with your little one beside you during the metamorphosis.

name: t99_ifs7
headline: AI Detected
windows: And the parts just keep coming: managers, firefighters, exiles, polarized parts, legacy burdens, Self-energy, guides, new subparts... At some point it’s a maze, with a little one somewhere in the middle of it.
Some practitioners are gentle about it and walk you through the maze just fine. Others seem to leave people more split up than when they started.
A big institute and a pile of certificates won’t tell you whether a model is true, or whether it’s safe for you.

name: t99_ifs_stretch
headline: AI Detected
windows: So inner child therapy draws on those higher vantage points more concretely. The inner Guide is the closest thing here to a Higher Self, and it has to work with the Nurturer and Protector and come after them.

It can’t act like some transcendent authority that waves everything away. Most reparenting doesn’t do enough with the Guide, which is the opposite extreme from IFS, so I’m trying to bring together the best of both.
IFS isn’t exactly one system, so I may be simplifying it here.
It has its own branches and disputes, and that’s one more problem I’m trying to remedy by laying all this out systematically in this guide.
IFS calls these wounded young parts “exiles.” I find that pathologizing.
I prefer to speak of a child who needs parenting and integration, rather than naming them by their wounded or excluded condition.
And the parts just keep coming: managers, firefighters, exiles, polarized parts, legacy burdens, Self-energy, guides, new subparts...
At some point it’s a maze, with a little one somewhere in the middle of it.

Some practitioners are gentle about it and walk you through the maze just fine. Others seem to leave people more split up than when they started. A big institute and a pile of certificates won’t tell you whether a model is true, or whether it’s safe for you.
